title: Assets and Liabilities
concept: Some things can generate income or increase in value, while others mainly require ongoing spending. Their financial role may depend on how they are used.
learningObjective: Understand the difference between things that may generate value and things that mainly cost money.
primaryMisconception: Every expensive item is automatically an asset.
secondaryMisconceptions: An item is always an asset or always a liability, regardless of how it is used.
Anything that earns money has no costs or financial risks.
keyTakeaway: The same item can play a different financial role depending on how it is used.

screens.title: One Bike, Two Money Stories
screens.content: Two identical bikes cost the same. One earns money; the other needs repairs. Can the same item play two different money roles?
screens.illustration: Two identical bikes split into separate paths. One carries paid deliveries, while the other sits beside a repair bill.

screens.title: Same Bike, Different Use
screens.content: Ava and Leo each receive the same bike. Ava uses hers for paid deliveries. Leo rides his only for weekend fun.
screens.illustration: Ava carries a delivery bag while Leo cycles through a park.

screens.title: Income and Costs
screens.content: Ava earns delivery money but still pays for tyres and repairs. Leo earns nothing from the bike and also pays maintenance costs.
screens.illustration: Coins enter Ava’s wallet while repair coins leave both Ava’s and Leo’s wallets.

screens.title: Price Is Not the Answer
screens.content: Now a computer, spare room, tools, and unused device appear. Their price alone will not reveal their financial role.
screens.illustration: Several item cards hide behind question marks labelled Income, Value, Use, and Costs.

screens.title: What Changes an Item’s Role?
screens.question: What should you check before deciding whether an item helps create value or mainly costs money?

options.text: How it is used, what it earns, and what it costs
options.response: Good thinking. An item’s price is only one clue. Its use, income, value, and running costs also matter.
An expensive item may lose value or create ongoing costs without producing income.
Appearance does not show whether the item earns money, keeps value, or costs more over time.
New items can still lose value quickly or create monthly costs.

screens.title: What Role Does It Play?
screens.instruction: Sort each example into Can Generate Value, Mainly Costs Money, or Depends on Use. Consider income, value, purpose, and ongoing costs.

educationalAssumptions: These examples show simplified financial roles.
A trusted adult manages paid work, renting, contracts, and payments.
Earning income does not guarantee that an item will be profitable.
Maintenance, repairs, subscriptions, and other costs must also be considered.
An item may move to another category if its use or costs change.
Future prices and income are not guaranteed.

categories.label: Can Generate Value
categories.description: Items that may earn income, support paid work, or provide lasting financial value under the stated conditions.

categories.label: Mainly Costs Money
categories.description: Items that do not currently earn income and mainly create purchase, subscription, repair, or maintenance costs.

categories.label: Depends on Use
categories.description: Items whose financial role changes depending on how they are used, what they earn, and what they cost.

sortableItems.title: Delivery Bike
sortableItems.example: A bike is used for paid deliveries with an adult’s supervision.
details: Average repairs and maintenance cost about £5 each week
The bike is needed to complete the deliveries
sortableItems.explanation: The bike supports paid work and earns more than its stated weekly costs in this example.

sortableItems.title: Rented Camera Equipment
sortableItems.example: Camera equipment is rented to a local school club through an adult-managed agreement.
details: It may remain valuable if cared for properly
sortableItems.explanation: The equipment may generate income and keep some value, although its costs and risks still need checking.

sortableItems.title: Repair Tool
sortableItems.example: A tool is used to provide a paid bicycle-repair service.
details: Requires replacement if damaged or worn out
sortableItems.explanation: The tool supports a service that earns money and may continue providing value over time.

sortableItems.title: Recreational Bike
sortableItems.example: A bike is used only for occasional weekend rides.
sortableItems.explanation: The bike may be enjoyable and useful, but its financial role in this example is mainly creating costs.

sortableItems.title: Unused Tablet
sortableItems.example: A tablet remains unused while an £8 monthly subscription continues.
details: Loses value as it becomes older
sortableItems.explanation: The device is not being used to create value and continues to reduce available money each month.

sortableItems.title: Status Trainers
sortableItems.example: Expensive trainers are purchased only to look fashionable.
details: May wear out or lose resale value
sortableItems.explanation: Their high price does not automatically make them an asset. In this example, they mainly create spending.

sortableItems.title: Family Car
sortableItems.example: A car may be used for family travel or for adult-managed paid work.
details: Personal use creates fuel, insurance, and repair costs
Income may or may not be greater than the running costs
sortableItems.explanation: The same car may mainly cost money or help generate value depending on its use and total expenses.

sortableItems.title: Computer
sortableItems.example: A computer may be used for games, schoolwork, or adult-supervised paid design work.
details: Software, electricity, and repairs create costs
sortableItems.explanation: Its role depends on what it is used for and whether the value or income created is greater than its costs.

sortableItems.title: Spare Room
sortableItems.example: A spare room may remain empty, be used by the family, or be rented through an adult-managed arrangement.
details: An empty room may still have maintenance costs
Renting may create income and additional responsibilities
sortableItems.explanation: The room’s financial role changes with its purpose, income, costs, and responsibilities.

ambiguityExplanation: The same item can play different roles.
A bike used only for recreation mainly creates costs.
The same type of bike used for paid deliveries may help generate value.
A computer used only for gaming creates costs, while one used for paid work may generate income.
Income alone does not decide the result. Running costs, repairs, time, risks, and changing value also matter.
placementRules: Every item must be placed in one category.
Use the details provided for each example.
Consider both money coming in and money going out.
Each item has one recommended category in this activity.
The category applies to the stated use, not to every similar item.
config.validationMethod: Check all nine items after submission. Keep correctly sorted items in place and return incorrect items with a short explanation.
config.retryBehavior: Keep correctly sorted items in place. Return only incorrect items to the centre, provide one short hint, and allow unlimited retries.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present each item as a text card with three buttons: Can Generate Value, Mainly Costs Money, and Depends on Use.
accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Listen to the item’s use, possible income, and ongoing costs. Then choose the most suitable financial role.

feedback.success: Excellent sorting. You looked beyond price and checked how each item was used, what it earned, and what it cost.
feedback.incorrect: Check the item’s use again. Does it create income or value, mainly create costs, or change roles depending on the situation?
feedback.incomplete: Sort all nine items before checking your answer.

screens.title: What You Own—and What You Owe
screens.content: You sorted items by how they were used. An asset is something you own that has value and may generate income or rise in value. A liability is money you owe, such as a loan. An item that mainly creates costs is not technically always a liability, but any debt used to buy it may be. Price alone does not decide an item’s role. Income, changing value, maintenance, and purpose all matter.
screens.simpleSummary: Check what an item earns, costs, is worth, and how it is used.
screens.illustration: A balance board separates things owned, money earned, running costs, and money owed. The same bike appears in two different roles.

screens.title: The Family Printer
screens.content: A family printer is used only for occasional homework and requires ink, so it mainly creates costs. Later, an adult uses it for a small paid invitation-printing service. It can then generate value—but ink, paper, electricity, and repairs still reduce the money earned.
screens.illustration: The printer changes from a homework-only card to a paid-printing card, while supply costs remain visible.

questions.text: Which item is most likely to generate value in the situation described?

options.text: A laptop used for paid design work
options.feedback: Correct. The laptop supports a service that earns income, although its costs must still be considered.

options.text: An unused phone with a monthly subscription
options.feedback: The phone is not creating income and continues to produce a monthly cost.
Their price or appearance does not automatically make them an income-producing asset.

options.text: A broken device kept in storage
options.feedback: The device is not currently producing income or useful financial value.

questions.correctExplanation: The laptop supports a service that earns income, although software, repairs, and other costs must still be considered.
questions.misconceptionTested: Anything expensive automatically creates financial value.

questions.text: A watch costs £2,000. Does its high price automatically make it an asset that improves someone’s finances?

options.text: No, its use, value, income, and costs still matter
options.feedback: Correct. Price alone does not show whether the watch improves someone’s finances.

options.text: Yes, because every expensive item is an asset
options.feedback: An expensive purchase can still lose value or mainly create ongoing spending.

options.text: Yes, because high prices always rise
options.feedback: An item’s future price may rise, fall, or stay similar. An increase is not guaranteed.

options.text: Yes, even if it quickly loses value
options.feedback: Losing value can weaken the item’s financial role even when its original price was high.

questions.correctExplanation: An expensive item may lose value, create costs, or produce no income. Price alone does not show whether it improves someone’s finances.
questions.misconceptionTested: Every expensive item is automatically an asset.

questions.text: A family car earns £200 from paid work but costs £170 for fuel, repairs, and other work-related expenses. What should the family consider?

options.text: The £30 remaining and whether other costs or risks exist
options.feedback: Correct. Income should be compared with every related cost and risk.
Income alone does not show the result. The £170 of costs must also be included.
The purchase price matters, but ongoing income, fuel, repairs, and other costs also affect the car’s role.
Profit is what remains after related costs. The full £200 is not profit when £170 was spent.

questions.correctExplanation: The income must be compared with all related costs. In this simplified example, £30 remains before considering any additional expenses or risks.
questions.misconceptionTested: Anything that earns money has no costs or financial risks.

screens.headline: Value Role Detective!
screens.message: You learned why price alone does not decide whether something generates value or mainly creates costs.
screens.progressMessage: Mission 13 complete in Make Money Grow.
screens.nextMissionTeaser: Next, explore why possible financial rewards often come with uncertainty and risk.

screens.title: Give One Item Two Roles
screens.instruction: Choose one household item. Write one way it could mainly create costs and one safe, adult-managed way it could generate value. No transaction is required.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on how an item’s financial role depends on its use, value, income, and costs.
The mission distinguishes assets from liabilities and clarifies that a cost-producing item is not technically always a liability.
The mission uses bikes, computers, trainers, tools, rooms, and family examples with simple income-and-cost comparisons.
The mission teaches a general concept without recommending the purchase, sale, or rental of any real item.
The mission states that income, rental demand, future value, and paid work are not guaranteed.
The mission does not discuss stocks or financial markets.
Recreational and status purchases are described by their financial role without presenting enjoyment or personal choices as morally wrong.
The mission explains that assets are things owned with value, liabilities are amounts owed, and an item’s financial role can change with its use.
The mission uses pounds and familiar UK examples such as bikes, cars, computers, subscriptions, tools, and spare rooms.
The learner sorts identical or similar items according to their income, costs, value, and use.
The quiz addresses expensive purchases, income-producing items, running costs, and financial risks.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses three short story screens, nine concise sorting cards, and three quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The wording is concrete, supportive, and suitable for children aged 8–12.
